mcqs.question: Which of these best demonstrates dependency injection?
options: A class declares a dependency in its constructor and lets the caller decide what to pass
A class instantiates the concrete database implementation it needs inside its constructor
A class uses a static singleton to fetch its dependency internally, hiding it from callers
A class exposes a getter for a dependency it already created itself
mcqs.explanation: Injection means the object declares what it needs and the caller supplies it. Building the concrete implementation internally is exactly the hard-wiring DI avoids; a static singleton hides the dependency behind a global with the same substitution problem as `new`; exposing a getter afterward doesn't change who built the object.

mcqs.question: You have an optional logging dependency that most callers never set. Which injection style fits best?
options: Constructor injection, making the logger a required argument everywhere
Method injection, passing the logger on every single call
Hard-code a default logger inside the class and never inject it
Setter/property injection, so callers only wire it up when they want logging
mcqs.explanation: Setter/property injection fits optional, sometimes-present dependencies — callers who don't care about logging never have to supply anything. Forcing it into the constructor makes an optional thing mandatory everywhere; method injection is overkill for something that doesn't vary per call; hard-coding it reintroduces the original substitution problem.

mcqs.question: In the refactored NotificationService example, what specifically makes the class testable that the original version lacked?
options: The class now has fewer lines of code overall
The notify method's signature changed to accept the message as a parameter
The emailer is passed in as an abstraction the constructor accepts, instead of being built inside the class
The class now imports an interface instead of a concrete class in its source file
mcqs.explanation: Testability comes from the constructor accepting an Emailer abstraction supplied externally — a test can now pass a fake. Line count is incidental, notify's signature was unchanged, and merely importing an interface without injecting it wouldn't help if the class still built its own instance.

mcqs.question: A code reviewer flags a constructor that takes eleven injected dependencies. What's the actual problem being pointed out?
options: Eleven dependencies makes the class impossible to unit test
The large constructor signals the class likely has too many responsibilities, not a DI problem
DI containers have a hard limit on constructor argument count
Constructor injection should be replaced with setter injection once you exceed five dependencies
mcqs.explanation: A huge constructor is still perfectly testable — the real signal is that the class is doing too much. Mocking all eleven dependencies is tedious but possible; there's no such container limit; swapping to setter injection would hide the smell instead of fixing the underlying responsibility overload.
